newsitem.title: PERU: Mothers cry out for bodies of dead Peru rebels.
newsitem.headline: Mothers cry out for bodies of dead Peru rebels.

text.p: Mothers of Tupac Amaru rebels killed in Tuesday's bloody hostage rescue begged the Peruvian government on Thursday to hand the corpses over to their families.

"I beg with tears in my eyes that the body of my son be returned to me. He is dead now, I beg you," pleaded Maria de Rojas, mother of the hostage-takers' second-in-command Rolly Rojas, known as "the Arab".

The sobbing mother was one of a handful of women gathered in front of Lima's military hospital morgue, which housed the corpses of 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels killed by commandos in the raid to free 72 hostages.
"Please, mister president. I beg you from my heart ... let me see him," she said in front of local television cameras.
While the mothers were reduced to pleading for their children's bodies, the two army commados killed in the raid were buried with full military honours on live television.
All 14 guerrillas and one of the 72 hostages died in the furious gunbattle inside the residence, occupied by the rebels on Dec. 17 to demand freedom for their jailed comrades.
The rebels killed in the raid included several teenagers. Only one, operation leader Nestor Cerpa, was older than 25, local news reports said.
Officials said any order to release the bodies would have to come from a senior government official. "The order has not arrived. The order must come from up high," an employee of the morgue said.
Though President Alberto Fujimori has said he would allow the bodies to be turned over to relatives, the mother of teenage rebel hostage-taker Giovanna Vila said authorities were dragging their feet.
Hospital authorities "demand more and more things, and what for? ... They aren't handing the bodies over," Vila's mother said, trembling with grief.

Members of local human rights group APRODEH came to the morgue late on Wedneseday after the mothers requested their help retrieving the corpses. Their efforts will continue "as long as it's necessary," said one APRODEH official.
Cerpa's mother said on local television from her home in the French city of Nantes that she wanted to return to Peru "to bury him and see him for the last time."
